IREKS summary of enzyme effects: amylases lower dough viscosity and feed the yeast (colour, volume); pentosanases/xylanases split insoluble carbohydrates, giving higher water binding, drier dough, more volume and better freshkeeping; proteases soften gluten and give a more tender, shorter crumb; lipases give more volume; hexose oxidases produce hydrogen peroxide that strengthens gluten and dries the dough.

claim: Bakery protease is dosed at 0.1–0.5 % of flour depending on product (e.g. 0.25 % powder or 75 haemoglobin units per 100 g flour), works best at pH 4.5–6.5, and in excess weakens the gluten so much that gas retention falls; it is mainly used in processes without long fermentation or sourdough.

Xylanase (EC 3.2.1.8) cuts the xylan backbone of arabinoxylans; partial breakdown of water-unextractable arabinoxylans into medium-to-high molecular weight water-extractable ones improves dough handling, gas retention, oven spring and crumb fineness, and releases water bound by the larger polymers (dough relaxation).

claim: Lipoxygenase is usually added as enzyme-active soy flour at no more than 0.5 %; it bleaches flour carotenoids (whiter crumb), co-oxidises proteins to strengthen the dough against over-mixing, and can create off-flavours if over-used.

Mills add ascorbic acid at 0.5–3.0 g per 100 kg flour (5–30 ppm). An enzyme of the flour converts it into dehydroascorbic acid, which oxidises the flour's glutathione and so stops glutathione from weakening the gluten; dough stability and gas retention rise.

claim: In bread and buns ascorbic acid is used up to 150 ppm of flour; the US FDA limit is 200 ppm. It needs oxygen from mixing and the flour's ascorbate oxidase to act, competes with yeast and glucose oxidase for oxygen, and whole-wheat or multigrain doughs need more of it. Historical work reported about 20 % more volume at 20–30 mg/kg.
notes: BAKERpedia also states an EU/UK maximum of 200 ppm except wholemeal; that statement was not checked against EU law.

claim: Glucose oxidase oxidises glucose into gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide; the peroxide strengthens gluten (disulphide and dityrosine cross-links, arabinoxylan gelation). It needs oxygen, so it acts mainly during mixing; the yeast soon uses up the dough's oxygen.

Most bakery lipases prefer pH about 8 and temperatures above 45 °C; they turn flour polar lipids into surface-active lysolipids. Over-dosing releases free fatty acids (rancid taste) and can break down the lysolipids again, with gas-cell coalescence and loss of oven spring.

Lowering whole-wheat dough to about pH 5.5, by sourdough or by adding lactic acid, broke down 70 % of the flour phytate, against 40 % without leavening or acidification: the wheat's own phytase, not the sourdough microbes, did most of the work.

Sourdough fermentation lowered phytate in whole-wheat bread by 62 %, yeast fermentation by 38 %; pre-incubating the bran with sourdough or yeast raised breakdown to about 90 %, whereas 40 % of the phytate remained in traditional French bread.
Endogenous cereal phytase works best at pH 4.3–5.5; an early sourdough study put the optimum for phytate degradation at pH 4.3–4.6.

source.locator: section on mineral bioaccessibility and Table (citing Fretzdorff 1992 and Leenhardt 2005)
source.author: Ribet et al.

claim: Long sourdough fermentation degrades much more phytate than short yeast fermentation, because acidification activates the flour's phytase and yeast has little phytase; whole-grain sourdoughs show the largest reductions; added fungal phytase (Aspergillus niger) can remove up to 100 %.

Roasting or cooking grain destroys its phytase, so fermenting cooked or roasted grain does not reduce phytate much; grains low in phytase (maize, rice, oats, millet) need longer fermentation or an addition of a high-phytase grain.

EFSA excluded from its evidence base β-glucans that had been degraded, for example by enzymatic hydrolysis, to lower molecular weight or viscosity, because such degradation lowers their post-prandial glucose-lowering efficacy.

claim: BAKERpedia recommends 1.8–2.0 % salt (baker's %) in bread and 0.75–1.25 % in cookies and cakes, where it is only for flavour. In bread, salt tightens the gluten (the more salt, the stiffer the dough) and slows the yeast by osmosis.

Adding 1.5 % salt to 176 Italian soft-wheat flours (41 cultivars) lowered farinograph water absorption by a few percentage points in 95 % of samples, lengthened development time in 78 % and raised stability in 70 %, lowered softening in 72 %, and raised alveograph strength W by up to 86 %.

The authors conclude that more than 1.5 % salt is unnecessary for bread-making quality.

claim: Salt's effect on fermentation rate is modelled in the fermentation model (modifier 'salt', from rheofermentometer gas data of the same study): about 4 % faster at 1.5 % salt and 12 % slower at 3 % than at 2 %.

Sugar feeds the yeast, sweetens, holds water (humectant, lower water activity), browns by Maillard reaction and caramelisation, and raises the temperature at which starch gelatinises and proteins denature; in short-time bread processes some fermentable sugar is needed for full proof and oven spring.

claim: Sweeteners raise the gelatinisation temperature of starch; wheat starch (onset 60.8 °C in water) is among the most affected. Fructose raises it least, isomalt and isomaltulose most, and the rise grows with concentration (tested at 0.5–4 M in a 2:1 solution:starch slurry).
notes: Quantitative shifts per sugar level are in the scalds/DSC part of the corpus (model-cereal.json).

claim: The slowing of yeast by high sugar levels (osmotic stress) is handled by the fermentation model's sugar modifier; osmotolerant instant yeast is the usual answer in sweet doughs.

Honey can replace sugar 1:1 by weight if the recipe's liquid is cut by 15–18 % of the honey weight; the oven should be about 14 °C cooler to limit browning. Honey's pH is 3.5–4.5, and fructose plus glucose make up 65–95 % of its carbohydrate.

Shortening is used at 3–5 % in bread to improve sliceability, moistness, volume and oven spring, up to 12 % in yeasted doughnuts; it shortens gluten strands and slows starch retrogradation. 100 g butter is replaced by 80 g shortening.
Butter is about 80 % fat; the remaining 20 % is water with milk solids. It interferes with gluten development, which makes baked goods more tender.

Compared with water, milk in a dough raises water absorption (softer dough), raises dough pH so fermentation is slower and more tolerant, browns faster (lactose), and gives more volume, a darker crust and longer shelf life. 100 g whole milk can be rebuilt from 8.5 g non-fat dry milk, 3.5 g butter and 88 g water.

Egg composition for bakers: liquid whole egg 75 % moisture (protein 53.2 %, fat 46.0 % of dry matter), liquid whites 88 % moisture, liquid yolks 49 % moisture (fat 62 % of dry matter), dried whole egg 5 % moisture. Eggs add colour, flavour, structure by protein coagulation, emulsification by yolk lecithin, and tenderness.

For hydration bookkeeping, count the water each ingredient brings: dough water = water + 0.89 × milk + 0.76 × whole egg + 0.55 × yolk + 0.88 × white + 0.15 × butter + 0.18 × honey + 0.21 × malt syrup. The dough will still feel softer than an all-water dough of the same hydration because fat and yolk tenderise and sugar competes for water.

Core-temperature endpoints for the app: lean and enriched wheat pan loaves and rolls 88–96 °C (88 °C gives the softest crumb, 96–98 °C a firmer one that holds its shape); hearth loaves 96–99 °C; rye and gluten-free breads 96–99 °C and then a long rest; thin crusty breads by crust colour (the core is already ~100 °C).

claim: Steam condenses on the dough surface, heats it fast and keeps it extensible so the loaf can expand evenly; without steam the crust tears irregularly and stays matt. Rye and mixed rye breads need the steam let out after a short time so a stable crust forms, otherwise the crust cracks. Under-proofed pieces and hot ovens need more steam; over-proofed pieces and cool ovens less (IREKS scale from 1 = least, over-proof in a cool oven, to 5 = most, under-proof in a hot oven).

Bake loss is higher for free-standing (oven-bottom) loaves than for touching or tin-baked ones because of the larger crust; higher for small pieces, for long narrow shapes than for round compact ones, and for longer bakes; a cooler oven, needing a longer bake, also raises it.

claim: Hamelman: a baked loaf can weigh 20 % or more less than its dough; larger pieces lose a smaller share, long thin loaves such as baguettes lose far more than round or oblong loaves of the same weight, pan breads lose less than hearth loaves, and a hotter oven gives less loss than a cooler one for the same piece.

No measured bake-loss figures for lidded pots (Dutch ovens) were found. By the stated mechanisms (exposed crust area, bake length, steam), a covered first phase should lose less than an open hearth bake of the same loaf, and a tin less again; use 20–24 % for open hearth loaves of 0.5–1 kg and 13–16 % for tin loaves until a user logs their own.

Staling starts as soon as bread cools: water moves from the crumb to the crust and out, the crust loses crispness and the crumb firms. Amylose retrogrades already during cooling and sets the initial crumb firmness; amylopectin recrystallises slowly during storage and squeezes out water (synaeresis). Amylose retrogradation is irreversible; amylopectin retrogradation can be partly reversed by reheating ('crisping up'), which gives a short-lived impression of freshness.

Recrystallisation of bread starch is fastest around 0 °C. Freezing delays it; so would warm storage above 55 °C at about 80 % relative humidity, but that costs energy and risks spoilage. Freezing pre-baked and baked goods at −18 °C is the established practice.

source.locator: Bread ageing and freshkeeping > Measures to delay staling
source.author: IREKS GmbH

claim: For starch gels at bread-like water contents, retrogradation proceeds between the glass transition (about −5 °C) and the melting temperature of the crystallites (about 60 °C); nucleation is fastest near the glass transition, so refrigerator temperatures speed firming.

Over 10 days, crumb firmness rose to 424 % (wheat pan bread) and 398 % (rye-wheat sourdough bread) of the day-0 value in a plastic bag in the fridge (8.2 °C), against 390 % and 330 % in a plastic bag at room temperature (21.9 °C); a micro-perforated paper bag gave the second-fastest firming because the bread dried out.
conditions: commercial German breads, sliced daily from the open end

claim: Absolute moisture loss after 10 days (wheat pan bread / rye-wheat sourdough bread): micro-perforated paper bag 10.3 / 13.5 %, metal bread box 7.0 / 8.9 %, plastic bag at room temperature 3.5 / 5.7 %, plastic bag in the fridge 3.1 / 5.5 %.

Wheat pan bread in a plastic bag at room temperature showed visible mould from day 4–5, in a bread box (89 % RH) from day 4–6, and none in 10 days in a plastic bag in the fridge at 8 °C; the rye-wheat sourdough bread (pH 4.48) moulded only in the plastic bag at room temperature, after 10 days. A mouldy slice placed with it contaminated the sourdough bread in 4–5 days.

claim: USDA FSIS: bread and baked goods with mould should be discarded because porous foods can be contaminated below the surface. Visible mould is only part of the organism: its root threads can reach deep into a food, poisonous substances are often in and around these threads, and toxins may spread through the food. FSIS separates foods: hard cheese and firm, low-moisture vegetables may be used after cutting away at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) around and below the spot, and hard salami may be scrubbed, but bread, soft cheese, yogurt, cooked grains and other high-moisture foods are discarded; for jams, microbiologists advise against scooping out the mould and using the rest.

source.locator: sections 'Are Molds Only on the Surface of Food?' and table 'FOOD | HANDLING | REASON' (row 'Bread and baked goods: Discard')
source.author: U.S. Department of Agriculture

claim: BfR (German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment): foods with mould should not be eaten or left standing but disposed of at once, because moulds can form mycotoxins; bread is among the most susceptible foods. The only exceptions are air-dried sausage and whole hams, where mouldy parts are cut away generously. Mould threads (hyphae) spread inside a food before they are visible, and almost all mycotoxins are heat- and acid-stable, so cooking, frying or acid pickling does not remove them.

source.locator: questions 'Woran sind Schimmelpilze zu erkennen?', 'Wie geht man mit Lebensmitteln um, die sichtbar von Schimmelpilzen befallen sind?' and 'Was sind Schimmelpilzgifte (Mykotoxine)?'

claim: Neither USDA FSIS nor BfR addresses sourdough starters. A starter is a moist, porous flour paste, which FSIS groups with the foods to discard when mouldy (high moisture, contamination below the surface), and BfR advises disposing of any visibly mouldy food except dry-cured meats; neither the starter's acidity nor the heat of baking would remove mycotoxins, which BfR describes as heat- and acid-stable. By these authorities' reasoning a visibly mouldy starter is discarded rather than rescued from an unaffected part, which contradicts baking-book advice to save it.
conditions: visible mould (fuzzy growth) on a starter, not the grey liquid ('hooch') or a dried skin

claim: IREKS measures to keep bread fresh longer: higher dough yields (more water in the crumb), sponges and sourdoughs (longer swelling and enzymatic breakdown of starch), a hot start with falling heat and a shorter bake (more water left in the crumb than a long bake at lower heat), enzyme improvers that cut starch during baking, emulsifiers, guar gum, and enzyme-active malt flour.

claim: Anti-staling options: emulsifiers do not make fresh bread softer but slow its firming; maltogenic amylases of intermediate heat stability produce dextrins that hinder starch realignment; lipases; hydrocolloids; high sugar (raises the glass transition); long fermentations such as sourdough or sponges; freezing; packaging; and larger, thicker products, which stale more slowly than small flat ones.

claim: Wheat rolls lose crispness within hours and are eaten soon after baking; rye and mixed rye breads keep fresh for several days, and freshkeeping improves with the rye share. Coarse rye bread is given a maturing time after cooling because fresh crumb is still slightly sticky.

Chinese steamed bread stored 2 days at 4 °C (or cycled 4 °C/25 °C) formed more ordered starch double helices than at 25 °C or −18 °C and had the slowest in-vitro starch digestion; storage at −18 °C gave fewer, more heterogeneous double helices.
conditions: steamed bread from several wheat varieties

claim: In King Arthur's tests, loaves baked only to 190 °F (88 °C) stayed moister for a couple of days than the same loaves baked to 205 °F (96 °C), and lightly baked buns stayed moist for several days while longer-baked ones dried out.
conditions: home bakes, one loaf per condition

claim: Reheating stale crumb above the melting range of retrograded amylopectin (about 60 °C) re-softens it for a short time; the effect fades as it cools because amylopectin recrystallises again and the amylose part never melts back at these temperatures. Re-crisping cannot replace water already lost.

Storage choice for the app: eat within a day or two at room temperature in a bag or box that limits drying; freeze (−18 °C) what will not be eaten in that window and reheat from frozen; the fridge slows mould but firms the crumb faster than room temperature.

A meta-analysis of 18 trials in adults (to June 2021) found a smaller rise in blood glucose after sourdough bread than after industrially fermented bread or a glucose drink: mean difference in the change of serum glucose −0.29 (95 % CI −0.46 to −0.12; I² = 0 %) at 60 min and −0.21 (−0.32 to −0.09; I² = 0 %) at 120 min. Certainty of evidence was low to very low; sourdough did not change fasting insulin or PYY, and the effect was clearest for whole-wheat sourdough.
conditions: randomised parallel or crossover trials; comparators pooled: industrial bread or glucose
notes: Units of the mean difference are not stated in the abstract (serum glucose, presumably mmol/L). Pooling glucose as a comparator is the design EFSA judges uninformative (see efsa2014).

claim: EFSA (2014) assessed a claim that high-fibre sourdough rye bread reduces post-prandial glycaemic responses: the four studies showed lower glucose responses than glucose, but almost any carbohydrate food does the same at equal available carbohydrate, so the effect was not specific; conditions of use could not be established. EFSA repeated this reasoning in 2025.
conditions: health-claim assessment under Article 13(5) of Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006

claim: A 2026 systematic review of 27 human studies in healthy adults, following the EFSA dossier framework, concluded that the evidence for a beneficial effect of sourdough over yeast-fermented bread on glycaemic and insulinaemic homeostasis is neither sufficient nor convincing; no meta-analysis was done because designs, outcomes and risk of bias differed too much.

A 2023 systematic review found 20 studies of sourdough bread and glucose response (369 people). In healthy subjects, 3 of 8 comparisons of the same recipe with sourdough or yeast showed a significantly lower glucose response with sourdough and 5 showed none; of 7 comparisons of whole-grain sourdough with white yeast bread, 2 were significant and 5 were not.
notes: Counts from the text: one Swedish study plus two further studies significant, five not.

claim: A 2017 review of human studies concluded that sourdough fermentation instead of baker's yeast can modulate the glucose response to bread, possibly through organic acids, while its effect on insulin is less clear; other process changes (cooking method, proofing period, partial baking and freezing) can also lower the glucose response.

In 10 healthy adults, the 2-h incremental glucose area after homemade white bread fell from 259 mmol·min/L fresh to 179 when frozen and defrosted, 193 when toasted and 157 when frozen, defrosted and toasted; for a commercial white bread it fell from 253 fresh to 183 toasted and 187 frozen-defrosted-toasted.
notes: Relative reductions: -31 %, -25 %, -39 % (homemade); -28 %, -26 % (commercial). Small single study.

claim: Gelatinised starch that is cooled retrogrades into type-3 resistant starch, which escapes digestion in the small intestine; the review gives a minimum of about 12 h of cooling and states that reheating below 130 °C does not turn it back into digestible starch. In cooked potatoes resistant starch rose from 0.64 g/100 g to 1.30 g/100 g after 24 h at 4 °C and to 1.65 g/100 g after reheating.
conditions: narrative review; potato example, not bread

claim: For bread, cooling, freezing and toasting lower the glucose response in a small human study and storage at 4 °C slows in-vitro starch digestion, but no measured resistant-starch content (g per 100 g) of cooled, frozen or toasted bread was found in the sources read; the app should describe the direction of the effect and the study sizes, not promise a resistant-starch amount or a GI value.

In order to bear the claim information shall be given to the consumer that the beneficial effect is obtained with a daily intake of 3 g of beta-glucans from oats, oat bran, barley, barley bran, or from mixtures of these beta-glucans."

In order to bear the claim information shall be given to the consumer that the beneficial effect is obtained by consuming the beta-glucans from oats or barley as part of the meal."

claim: EFSA (2025) rejected lowering the post-prandial claim's condition from 4 g to 2 g of oat or barley β-glucan per 30 g of available carbohydrate: across 21 studies (59 comparisons) and dose–response meta-regressions, effects at 2 to <4 g were not consistent and the lowest effective dose appeared to lie above 2 g.

What the claims mean for a loaf: bread holds about 44–54 g available carbohydrate per 100 g (Ciqual: wholemeal 44.3, average bread 54.4), so the post-prandial claim needs about 5.9–7.3 g oat or barley β-glucan per 100 g of bread, while the cholesterol claim needs 1 g per stated portion (2 g per 100 g for a 50 g portion). Flour or bran weight is not β-glucan weight, and β-glucan can be degraded during fermentation.

Regulation (EU) 432/2012, claim 'Replacing digestible starches with resistant starch in a meal contributes to a reduction in the blood glucose rise after that meal': "The claim may be used only for food in which digestible starch has been replaced by resistant starch so that the final content of resistant starch is at least 14 % of total starch."

claim: Straight-dough processing leaves about 1–1.5 % fructans in wheat bread and about 3 % in rye bread. Baker's yeast invertase degrades mainly short fructans (DP up to about 4), so long-chain fructans survive; conventional sourdoughs lower FODMAPs but can create new ones (mannitol from fructose). Low-FODMAP bread needs organisms with extracellular fructanase.

In a randomised double-blind crossover trial in people with IBS, a low-FODMAP rye bread made with a fructanase-active sourdough (FODMAPs cut to one third, dietary fibre kept at 10 g/100 g) caused less flatulence, abdominal pain, cramps and stomach rumbling than regular rye bread; a second trial found less breath hydrogen.

claim: A whole-grain bread process with 6 % baker's yeast plus baking powder, fermented 60 min at 40 °C, cut FODMAP content by more than 75 %.

No single curve of fructan loss against fermentation time holds across flours: in refined wheat a longer yeast proof lowers fructans, in rye 90–180 min of yeast fermentation does not, and sourdough trades fructans for mannitol unless the organisms carry fructanase. The app can say that longer or yeast-rich fermentation tends to lower wheat fructans, but should not label a bread low-FODMAP without analysis.

Regular sourdough bread is not gluten-free: fermentation lowers gluten but not to 20 ppm or less, the US gluten-free limit. Beyond Celiac does not recommend sourdough for people with coeliac disease unless it is labelled gluten-free or made with gluten-free starter and ingredients, and notes that intestinal damage can occur without symptoms.

In the EU, 'gluten-free' may only be stated for food that contains no more than 20 mg/kg of gluten as sold, and 'very low gluten' for specially processed wheat, rye, barley or oat ingredients at no more than 100 mg/kg.

In a 60-day trial in people with coeliac disease eating 200 g of baked goods a day, ordinary wheat flour (80,127 ppm gluten) made 2 of 6 stop because of symptoms, with rising anti-transglutaminase antibodies and small-bowel deterioration; extensively hydrolysed flour (2,480 ppm residual gluten) caused no complaints but subtotal villous atrophy in both patients; only fully hydrolysed flour (8 ppm), made with selected sourdough lactobacilli plus fungal proteases, left antibodies and mucosa unchanged in 5 patients.

An acute challenge used a sourdough of 30 % wheat with oat, millet and buckwheat flours, fermented 24 h with selected lactobacilli and their extracts, about 2 g gluten per bread: 13 of 17 coeliac patients showed altered intestinal permeability after the yeast bread but not after this sourdough bread.

Sourdough fermentation does not make wheat, rye or barley bread safe for people with coeliac disease. Ordinary sourdough leaves gluten far above the 20 mg/kg gluten-free limit; the experimental breads that coeliac patients tolerated used selected lactobacilli plus fungal proteases (or mostly gluten-free flours) and reached 8 ppm, while partly hydrolysed flour at 2,480 ppm still damaged the intestine.
conditions: applies to spelt, einkorn, emmer and khorasan wheats too

claim: A 2026 systematic review of 8 human intervention studies found the effect of sourdough or phytate reduction on iron inconclusive: single meals showed better absorption (low-phytate white bread raised serum iron by 59 vs 30 µg/100 mL for high-phytate wholemeal; added phytase raised iron absorption by 50 % for ferrous sulfate and 61 % for iron bis-glycinate), but over 12 weeks a low-phytate sourdough rye bread did not improve iron status (ferritin 32 ± 7 → 27 ± 6 µg/L; body iron 6.9 → 5.4 mg/kg).

More free minerals after in-vitro digestion of fermented dough (bioaccessibility) does not prove better absorption or mineral status: residual phytate is partly broken down in the stomach and, by microbial phytases, in the colon, where most phytate degradation in the body takes place.
